text: Sir James Augustus Henry Murray, FBA (/ˈmʌri/; 7 February 1837 – 26 July 1915), was a British lexicographer and philologist who served as the primary editor of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) from 1879 until his death. Born in Denholm near Hawick in the Scottish Borders, he was the eldest son of a draper, Thomas Murray, and had brothers Charles Oliver Murray and A. D. Murray, who later edited the Newcastle Daily Journal. He was christened James Murray but adopted the names Augustus Henry in 1855 to distinguish himself from other James Murrays in the Hawick area. A precocious and avid learner, he left school at fourteen due to financial constraints and became a teacher at Hawick Grammar School at seventeen, later serving as headmaster of the Subscription Academy three years later. In 1856, he co-founded the Hawick Archaeological Society. In 1861, he met music teacher Maggie Scott, whom he married the following year; they had a daughter, Anna, who died of tuberculosis, followed by Maggie’s illness, prompting the couple to move to London to escape the Scottish winters. Murray took an administrative job with the Chartered Bank of India while pursuing academic interests, but Maggie died within a year of arriving in London. He then engaged to Ada Agnes Ruthven, married her the following year, and her best man was Alexander Graham Bell, who had received instruction from Murray in elementary electricity and referred to him as "the grandfather of the telephone." Murray’s linguistic expertise included an 'intimate acquaintance' with Italian, French, Catalan, Spanish, and Latin, and 'to a lesser degree' Portuguese, Vaudois, Provençal, and various dialects; he was 'tolerably familiar' with Dutch, German, and Danish, had 'much closer' studies of Anglo-Saxon and Mœso-Gothic, knew 'a little of the Celtic,' was 'engaged with the Slavonic' and had obtained a useful knowledge of Russian, and had 'sufficient knowledge of Hebrew and Syriac to read and cite the Old Testament and Peshito,' with lesser knowledge of Aramaic, Arabic, Coptic, and Phoenician. He did not secure the job he applied for at the British Museum. By 1869, he was on the council of the Philological Society, and by 1873 had left the bank to return to teaching at Mill Hill School, where he published *The Dialect of the Southern Counties of Scotland*, enhancing his reputation in philological circles. In 1881, he was elected a member of the American Philosophical Society. Murray had eleven children with Ada, all bearing the surname Ruthven by arrangement with his father-in-law, George Ruthven; the eldest, Harold James Ruthven Murray, became a prominent chess historian, Sir Oswyn Murray served as permanent secretary at the Admiralty (United Kingdom) from 1917 to 1936, Robert Murray was a Jesuit priest and specialist in Syriac, and Wilfrid George Ruthven Murray wrote an account of his father. All eleven children survived to maturity, a rarity at the time, and assisted in the compilation of the OED. Murray died of pleurisy on 26 July 1915 and requested to be buried in Oxford beside the grave of his best friend, James Legge. On 26 April 1878, he was invited to Oxford to meet the Delegates of the Oxford University Press to take on the role of editor of a new English dictionary to replace Johnson’s and capture all existing words in their various meanings. On 1 March 1879, a formal agreement was made for Murray to edit a new English dictionary, which would eventually become the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), expected to take ten years to complete, span 7,000 pages in four volumes, but when finally published in 1928, it consisted of twelve volumes, containing 414,825 words defined and 1,827,306 citations. To prepare for the work, Murray built a corrugated-iron shed at Mill Hill School called the Scriptorium to house his assistants and the flood of slips (quotations illustrating word usage) that began to arrive from his appeals. As work progressed, he gave up teaching to become a full-time lexicographer. In the summer of 1884, Murray and his family moved to a large house on Banbury Road in north Oxford, where he built a larger Scriptorium in the back garden to accommodate the growing volume of slips. Anything addressed to "Mr Murray, Oxford" was delivered to him, and due to the volume of mail, the Post Office installed a special post box outside his house. Murray became president of the Oxford Philatelic Society, using his extensive collection of postage stamps from readers worldwide. Despite his dedication to the OED, which earned him a knighthood in 1908, he remained a relative outsider in Oxford, never joining university academic or Senior Common Room life, never becoming a Fellow of an Oxford college, and receiving an honorary doctorate only the year before his death. William Chester Minor was a major contributor to the OED, becoming one of the project’s most effective volunteers and drawing the attention of Murray, who visited him in January 1891. In 1899, Murray praised Minor’s contributions, stating, "we could easily illustrate the last four centuries from his quotations alone." The book *The Surgeon of Crowthorne*, published in 1998 as *The Professor and the Madman* by Simon Winchester, chronicles Minor’s life and contributions to the OED. The film rights were purchased by Mel Gibson’s Icon Productions in 1998, and Farhad Safinia directed the film adaptation, *The Professor and the Madman*, released in May 2019, starring Gibson as Murray and Sean Penn as Minor. In 2003, Winchester published *The Meaning of Everything: The Story of the Oxford English Dictionary*, which covers the origins and completion of the OED nearly seventy years after its inception. The novel *The Dictionary of Lost Words* (2020) by Australian author Pip Williams, set in the scriptorium where Murray and his team worked, became a best-selling book. Murray was awarded honorary doctoral degrees by nine universities, including one in 1899 when Minor provided 12,000 quotations for the OED.
